newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Cancer becoming top segment for Viaticus.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Cancer becoming top segment for Viaticus.

text.p: Viaticus Inc, a unit of CNA Financial Corp that buys life insurance policies from terminally ill people, expects to see cancer patients overtaking AIDS sufferers as the largest portion of its business by the end of next year.

"Certainly, Viaticus would expect that cancer would become the leading condition that we help by the end of next year," Viaticus president Gary Chodes said in a recent interview with Reuters. "Other companies probably aren't going to make the transition in the same way."

Viatical settlements, the process of buying a terminally ill patient's life insurance policy so the person can have cash for medical bills, living expenses and other needs, were spawned around the beginning of the decade with AIDS patients, Chodes said.
But "within AIDS, that market is becoming more mature and with some of the treatment protocols that come out, it makes some of the people with AIDS not eligible for viatical settlement," Chodes said.

In fact, publicly held Dignity Partners Inc said in July it was temporarily ceasing to process new applications from individuals diagnosed with HIV and AIDS while it further analyzes research results on AIDS treatments presented at the International AIDS conference this summer. Last week, the San Francisco-based company said that analysis was continuing.

Meanwhile, a provision in recently passed healthcare legislation would allow payment to patients expected to die within two years to be tax exempt. Chodes said he expects this to help expand use of viatical settlements to people other than AIDS patients.
He noted that cancer accounts for a far greater percentage of deaths in the United States than HIV infection.
"There isn't any particular reason why a cancer patient wouldn't be as good if not better candidate for" a viatical settlement, he said.
Viaticus estimates that, on an industry-wide basis, about $800 million in policies will be purchased through viatical settlement in 1996. That will jump to over $1 billion by 1998, it said.
"With this tax bill, that rate is going to rapidly increase," he said, adding that Viaticus, which buys close to a third of the $500 million in policies it considers, will grow with that business.
"We'll be a significant percentage of that number and the largest participant, we believe," Chodes said.

Viaticus pays 60 to 85 percent of the face value of a policy to a terminally ill person, maintains the premium on the policy, then collects the full value when the person dies. When Viaticus does not buy a policy, it is usually because the policyholder chooses to sell to another company or to not take a settlement at all, a spokesman said.
While 50 percent of Viaticus' business currently comes from AIDS patients, Chodes expects that to drop to 25 percent next year.

The company is growing its business through education campaigns with social workers, estate planners and others involved with finances of terminally ill patients. Viaticus is also marketing viatical settlement as an employee benefit to corporate benefits managers.
